summary.text: The Indus script, also called the Harappan script, is a corpus of symbols produced by the Indus Valley Civilisation, and it has not yet been deciphered.
Most inscriptions are extremely short, which makes it hard to judge whether they formed a writing system used to record the language or languages presumed spoken.
The symbols mostly appear on small stamp seals, impressions of seals and pottery graffiti, and no known bilingual inscription exists to help decipher the script.

facts.label: Seal size
facts.value: Most seals were just 2 to 3 centimetres on each side

facts.label: Reading direction
facts.value: Mostly right to left, according to most scholars

facts.label: Common sign
facts.value: The jar sign is the most frequently used

items.prompt: A codebreaker would love a text giving the same message in the Indus script and in a known language. What is the situation?

options.label: No such bilingual inscription is known
One exists, but the script changes too much over time to compare
Several exist but have never been published
One exists, but it is far too short to read

items.explain: There is no known bilingual inscription to help decipher the script, which shows no significant changes over time.

items.prompt: A researcher hopes to find Indus script on a surviving scroll of bark or leaves. What do the finds so far suggest?

options.label: Examples on bark and leaves are the most common
No examples have been found on such perishable materials
Examples on bark exist but leaves have not survived
Examples on textiles outnumber those on seals

items.explain: No extant examples of the Indus script have been found on perishable organic materials like papyrus, paper, textiles, leaves, wood, or bark.

items.prompt: An alphabet needs a few dozen letters, each standing for a sound. Why does the number of Indus signs argue against each sign being a sound symbol?

options.label: The signs show a lot of change from one century to the next
Most signs appear only on seals made of gold
With over 400 principal signs, there are too many for each to stand for a sound
The signs are all abstract with no pictures

items.explain: The number of principal signs is over 400, too large for each character to be a phonogram, so the script is generally believed to be logo-syllabic.

items.prompt: Animals such as bulls, elephants and the mythical unicorn appear beside the text on seals. Why might they be there?

options.label: To spell out the text in picture form
To record how many debts the owner had
To mark the seal as a royal tax receipt
To help people who could not read tell where a seal came from

items.explain: Animals accompanied the text on seals, possibly to help the illiterate identify the origin of a particular seal.

items.prompt: Inscribed seals stopped being used at Harappa around 1900 BCE. What does the evidence say about the script elsewhere?

options.label: It may have lasted longer elsewhere, as at Rangpur
It ended everywhere at exactly the same moment
It spread widely across the lands of Egypt
It was replaced at once by the Brahmi script

items.explain: At Harappa the use of the script largely ceased, but it may have endured longer in other regions such as Rangpur, Gujarat.

items.prompt: Scholars point to later markings on potsherds in southern India that resemble Indus signs. How settled is the question of what these symbols mean?

options.label: They are confirmed to be Indus script
There is no scholarly consensus on their meaning
They are confirmed to be Brahmi script
They are confirmed to be unrelated decoration

items.explain: There is no scholarly consensus on the meaning of these non-Brahmi symbols, though some scholars argue they developed from the Indus script.

paragraphs.heading: An unread script
paragraphs.text: The Indus script, also called the Harappan script, is a body of symbols made by the Indus Valley Civilisation. Most inscriptions are very short, so it is hard to tell whether the signs were true writing, used to record the language or languages people are presumed to have spoken. Despite many attempts, no one has deciphered it. No bilingual inscription is known that could help, and the script shows no major changes over time.

paragraphs.heading: Where the signs appear
paragraphs.text: The symbols turn up mostly on stamp seals and pottery, and also on tools, weapons and plates of bronze or copper. Most of the surviving texts are seals, the marks those seals left, and graffiti scratched on pottery. The seals were small and easy to carry, most just 2–3 centimetres on each side. Signs were carved, chiselled, embossed or painted onto materials ranging from terracotta and soapstone to copper, silver and gold. None has survived on perishable materials such as papyrus, cloth, wood or bark. As of 1977, about 90% of known inscribed objects came from sites in Pakistan along the Indus and its tributaries, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

paragraphs.heading: What the signs look like
paragraphs.text: Most characters are pictures of objects, local or general, or of things from nature, though many abstract signs exist too. Some signs are built from simpler picture signs, and some appear only as parts of larger signs. A few look like tally marks and are often read as early numbers. Seals often showed animals beside the text, such as elephants, bulls, water buffaloes, rhinoceros and a mythical unicorn, perhaps to help people who could not read tell where a seal came from. Most scholars agree the script was usually read from right to left, though some texts run left to right or in boustrophedon mode.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the signs
paragraphs.text: There are over 400 main signs, too many for each one to be a phonogram, so the script is generally thought to be logo-syllabic. The exact total is unclear, because experts disagree about whether some signs are separate or just versions of one sign. In the 1970s Iravatham Mahadevan listed 419 distinct signs, while in 2015 Bryan Wells estimated around 694. Just 67 signs make up 80 percent of all use, and the most common is the jar sign.

paragraphs.heading: Rise and fading
paragraphs.text: The earliest examples are on pottery and clay seal impressions from around 2800–2600 BCE, in the Early Harappan period. Digs at Harappa show that some signs grew out of potter's marks and graffiti from the earlier Ravi phase, about 3500–2800 BCE. In the Mature Harappan period, about 2600–1900 BCE, strings of signs are common on flat, rectangular stamp seals and many other objects. At Harappa the script largely stopped when inscribed seals went out of use around 1900 BCE, but it may have lasted longer elsewhere, such as at Rangpur in Gujarat. Seals and pottery fragments bearing the script, dated to about 2200–1600 BCE, are also known from the Daimabad culture in Maharashtra.

paragraphs.heading: Clues and theories
paragraphs.text: The first published seal with these symbols was a drawing by Alexander Cunningham in 1875. By 1992 about 4,000 inscribed objects had been found, some as far away as Mesopotamia. Some scholars see a connection between the Indus signs and the Brahmi script, but this has not been proven. Others, such as Gregory Possehl, see graffiti symbols from the Iron Age in central and south India and Sri Lanka as the script living on. Linguists including Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola have argued that it was related to a Dravidian language.
